value.stringValue: [{"text":"Four travellers must cross a bridge at night with one torch. At most two cross at a time and a pair moves at the slower person's pace. They take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes. What is the fastest total crossing time, and what is the schedule?"}]

[{"text":"**The fastest time is 17 minutes.**

## Schedule

| Step | Move | Time | Running total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 and 2 cross | 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 1 returns with the torch | 1 | 3 |
| 3 | 5 and 10 cross | 10 | 13 |
| 4 | 2 returns with the torch | 2 | 15 |
| 5 | 1 and 2 cross | 2 | 17 |

The two slowest walkers cross together, so their 10 minutes is paid only once. The two fastest handle all the torch returns.

The obvious plan of having the 1-minute person escort everyone takes 2 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 10 = 19 minutes, which is worse.

## Why 17 can't be beaten

The number of crossings is odd, because the torch must end on the far side. Three crossings can move at most 2 − 1 + 2 = 3 people net, so at least 5 crossings are needed.

- **The 5 and 10 never cross together.** Then one crossing costs at least 10, another costs at least 5, and at least 3 more cost at least 1 each. That gives at least 18.
- **The 5 and 10 cross together (10 min).** The 2-minute person must cross in a different crossing, costing at least 2.
  - With 7 or more crossings, the total is at least 10 + 2 + 5·1 = 17.
  - With exactly 5 crossings, the pattern is forced: two people forward, one back, two forward, one back, two forward. The other two forward trips cost 2 each only if both are {1, 2}. Then both 1 and 2 must each make a return trip, costing 1 + 2 = 3. The total is 10 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 17. If either of those forward trips includes the 5 or the 10 instead, the total is at least 19.

So no schedule beats 17 minutes."}]

[{"text":"Four travellers must cross a bridge at night with one torch. At most two cross at a time and a pair moves at the slower person's pace. They take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes. What is the fastest total crossing time, and what is the schedule?"}]

**The fastest time is 17 minutes.**

## Schedule

| Step | Move | Time | Running total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 and 2 cross | 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 1 returns with the torch | 1 | 3 |
| 3 | 5 and 10 cross | 10 | 13 |
| 4 | 2 returns with the torch | 2 | 15 |
| 5 | 1 and 2 cross | 2 | 17 |

The two slowest walkers cross together, so their 10 minutes is paid only once. The two fastest handle all the torch returns.

The obvious plan of having the 1-minute person escort everyone takes 2 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 10 = 19 minutes, which is worse.

## Why 17 can't be beaten

The number of crossings is odd, because the torch must end on the far side. Three crossings can move at most 2 − 1 + 2 = 3 people net, so at least 5 crossings are needed.

- **The 5 and 10 never cross together.** Then one crossing costs at least 10, another costs at least 5, and at least 3 more cost at least 1 each. That gives at least 18.
- **The 5 and 10 cross together (10 min).** The 2-minute person must cross in a different crossing, costing at least 2.
  - With 7 or more crossings, the total is at least 10 + 2 + 5·1 = 17.
  - With exactly 5 crossings, the pattern is forced: two people forward, one back, two forward, one back, two forward. The other two forward trips cost 2 each only if both are {1, 2}. Then both 1 and 2 must each make a return trip, costing 1 + 2 = 3. The total is 10 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 17. If either of those forward trips includes the 5 or the 10 instead, the total is at least 19.

So no schedule beats 17 minutes.
